entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time signal from $x(t)$ to $x(-t)$ by mapping every time location $t_0$ to $-t_0$ and recognizing reversal as negative time scaling in the time-domain operation sequence.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Reversal

blocks.text: Time reversal is the operation that mirrors a continuous-time signal across $t=0$. In this first pass, the only thing that changes is the time argument, so the signal values stay attached to their original heights.
Write the reversed signal as $y(t)=x(-t)$. The minus sign acts on time, not on amplitude, so this means "read the original signal backward in time" rather than "flip the signal values."

For the base case, a point at $t_0=3$ moves to $-3$, and a point at $t_0=-2$ moves to $2$. The value attached to each point stays the same, so the reversal is a left-right swap in time, not a change in height.

You can also think of time reversal as time scaling by $-1$. That viewpoint will matter later, but for now the key idea is simple: every time location $t_0$ maps to $-t_0$ while the signal value itself is preserved.

sections.section_title: Evaluating Values of $x(-t)$ from $x(t)$

example_content.example_prompt: A signal is given by the table $x(-3)=4$, $x(-1)=1$, $x(0)=0$, and $x(2)=5$. For $y(t)=x(-t)$, find $y(3)$, $y(1)$, and $y(-2)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a lookup in $y(t)=x(-t)$. To answer it, flip the query time first and then read the matching value from the original $x(t)$ table.
Now read those values from the table: $x(-3)=4$, $x(-1)=1$, and $x(2)=5$.
So $y(3)=4$, $y(1)=1$, and $y(-2)=5$. The time argument changes sign, but the signal value itself does not.

sections.section_title: Mapping Time Locations Under Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Given labeled time locations at $t=-4$, $t=-1$, $t=0$, and $t=5$ on $x(t)$, trace the locations of the same features in $x(-t)$ and list the mirrored times in order.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a set of labeled times on $x(t)$. Under time reversal, each time coordinate flips sign, so the feature values stay attached while the locations move to the opposite side of $t=0$.
So the mirrored locations are $4$, $1$, $0$, and $-5$. The value attached to each feature does not change; only the time label changes sign.
Ordered from left to right, the reversed signal has features at $-5$, $0$, $1$, and $4$. The point at $0$ stays fixed because $-0=0$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Time Reversal as Scaling by $-1$

example_content.example_prompt: A student sees $y(t)=x(-t)$ and thinks it is a shift. Use a labeled point such as $t_0=6$ to show the point moves to $-6$ and explain why the operation is time scaling by $-1$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the minus sign inside the time argument. That means the transformation is of the form $y(t)=x(at)$ with $a=-1$, so time is being scaled, not shifted.
Use the tracked point $t_0=6$. Under the scaling rule, $6$ maps to $-6$, so the same feature appears at the mirrored time.
A shift would add the same offset to every time label, but here the sign of each time label changes instead. That is why the whole signal mirrors about $t=0$ and $0$ stays fixed.
So $y(t)=x(-t)$ is time scaling by $-1$, not a shift. The signal values stay attached to the same features while the time locations reverse.

entries.lesson_core_move: Reflect the graph of $x(t)$ across $t=0$ by moving each feature at time $t_0$ to $-t_0$ while preserving its amplitude.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Reflecting a Signal Across $t=0$

image_slots.image_description: A sparse continuous-time signal plot centered at $t=0$ showing one isolated feature at a positive time and its reflected location at the corresponding negative time. Include a vertical mirror line at $t=0$, clear $t$-axis and amplitude axis labels, and visible labels for $x(t)$ and $x(-t)$. Keep the plot clean, instructional, and uncluttered.

blocks.text: Reflecting a signal across $t=0$ means reading the graph left to right on the other side of the vertical axis. In $x(-t)$, every feature keeps the same amplitude but moves from time $t_0$ to time $-t_0$.
Start with one isolated feature at a positive time. If the feature sits at $t_0$, its mirror in $x(-t)$ sits at $-t_0$ with the same height, so the sign change belongs to time, not to amplitude.
That same rule applies to every other time location on the graph. A feature already on $t=0$ does not move, because $0$ changes to $-0$, which is still $0$.

So the first step is simple: find the mirror line at $t=0$, flip each time coordinate, and leave each amplitude unchanged. Later examples will reuse this same sign-flip rule with more features, but the base move is already complete here.

sections.section_title: Reflecting a Single Graph Feature Across $t=0$

image_slots.image_description: A clean two-panel instructional figure with identical axes and scale in both panels. The left panel shows $x(t)$ with one isolated peak at $t=3$ and height $2$. The right panel shows $x(-t)$ with the same peak mirrored to $t=-3$ and the same height $2$. Include a vertical mirror line at $t=0$, clear $t$-axis and amplitude axis labels, and no extra features or decoration.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a graph of $x(t)$ with one isolated peak at $t=3$ and height $2$, reflect the graph across $t=0$ to obtain $x(-t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single isolated peak at a positive time. To reflect across $t=0$, move that peak to the mirrored negative time and keep its height and shape unchanged.
For this graph, the peak at $t=3$ with height $2$ moves to $t=-3$ with the same height. The only change is the sign of the time coordinate.
The height stays $2$, and the shape stays the same, because reflection across $t=0$ changes time location but not amplitude.
So the reflected graph is the same peak on the left side of $t=0$, now located at $t=-3$ with height $2$.

sections.section_title: Reflecting a One-Sided Signal Segment Across $t=0$

image_slots.image_description: A clean two-panel instructional figure with identical axes and scale in both panels. The left panel shows $x(t)$ as a right-sided triangular segment on $0 \le t \le 4$ with a peak at $t=2$. The right panel shows $x(-t)$ as the mirrored left-sided segment on $-4 \le t \le 0$ with the same peak at $t=-2$. Include a vertical mirror line at $t=0$, clear $t$-axis and amplitude axis labels, and no extra decoration.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a right-sided triangular segment on $0 \le t \le 4$ with a peak at $t=2$, reflect the entire segment across $t=0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a connected segment on the positive-time side. To reflect it across $t=0$, move the whole segment to the negative-time side and keep the same interior shape.

For this segment, the left endpoint at $t=0$ stays fixed, the right endpoint at $t=4$ moves to $t=-4$, and the peak at $t=2$ moves to $t=-2$. The segment is the same triangle, just read in reverse order.
The heights do not change. Each interior point lands at the mirrored negative time, so the triangle keeps its shape while its support interval flips horizontally.
So the reflected signal is the same triangular segment on $-4 \le t \le 0$, with the peak now at $t=-2$ and the same height as before.

sections.section_title: Reflecting Multiple Graph Features Across $t=0$

image_slots.image_description: A clean two-panel instructional figure with identical axes and scale in both panels. The left panel shows $x(t)$ with three separated features: a pulse at $t=-2$, a dip at $t=1$, and a short flat segment from $t=3$ to $t=4$. Draw a vertical mirror line at $t=0$. The right panel shows $x(-t)$ with the pulse at $t=2$, the dip at $t=-1$, and the flat segment from $t=-4$ to $t=-3$. Use the same amplitudes and shapes in both panels, label the $t$-axis and amplitude axis clearly, and include no extra decoration.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a graph with a pulse at $t=-2$, a dip at $t=1$, and a short flat segment from $t=3$ to $t=4$, reflect the whole graph across $t=0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is several separated features on both sides of $t=0$. Start by listing each feature and its time coordinate, then reflect the graph by negating every time coordinate while keeping every amplitude and shape the same.
The pulse at $t=-2$ moves to $t=2$, the dip at $t=1$ moves to $t=-1$, and the flat segment from $t=3$ to $t=4$ moves to $t=-4$ to $t=-3$. The features switch sides, but none of their heights change.
After the reflection, rebuild the graph in left-to-right order on the new time locations. The flat segment now appears on the left, the dip sits at $t=-1$, and the pulse sits at $t=2$.
This is the complete reflection: every visible feature moved to its mirrored time, and nothing was skipped or duplicated.

sections.section_title: Reflecting Features That Lie on $t=0$

image_slots.image_description: A clean two-panel instructional figure with identical axes and scale in both panels. The left panel shows $x(t)$ with a spike exactly at $t=0$ and matching pulses at $t=-2$ and $t=2$. Draw a vertical mirror line at $t=0$. The right panel shows $x(-t)$ with the spike still at $t=0$ and the same matching pulses still at $t=-2$ and $t=2$. Use the same amplitudes and shapes in both panels, label the $t$-axis and amplitude axis clearly, and include no extra decoration.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a graph with a feature on $t=0$ and matching features at $t=\pm 2$, reflect the signal across $t=0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a feature on $t=0$ together with a matching pair on either side of the axis. The rule is that $t=0$ is a fixed point, so the on-axis feature stays in place while every off-axis feature moves to the opposite side with the same amplitude and shape.

The feature at $t=0$ does not move. The feature at $t=-2$ moves to $t=2$, and the feature at $t=2$ moves to $t=-2$. Because the off-axis pair matches, the reflected graph keeps the same overall appearance off the axis even though the time coordinates swap.
Rebuild the graph by leaving the axis feature where it is and placing each off-axis feature on the mirrored side. Nothing on $t=0$ changes position, and nothing off the axis changes amplitude.
So the special case is simple: a feature on $t=0$ stays fixed, and the usual reflection rule still applies to every other feature.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time piecewise definition $x(t)$ into the correctly ordered interval definition for $x(-t)$ by reflecting each breakpoint across $t=0$ and substituting $-t$ into the segment formulas.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Reversal of Piecewise Signals

blocks.text: A piecewise signal is read as formulas attached to time intervals. To reverse time, replace every $t$ with $-t$ and then rewrite the breakpoint locations so the intervals run from left to right in the new time variable.
Here the breakpoint at $t=2$ moves to $t=-2$. That means the right-hand piece in $x(t)$ becomes the left-hand piece in $x(-t)$, because the time axis has been reflected across $t=0$.

Read the result in increasing time order: first the interval on the left, then the next one. The rule to reuse is simple: reflect the breakpoints, substitute $-t$ into each piece, and reorder the intervals.

sections.section_title: Reflecting Breakpoints in a Piecewise Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Given a piecewise signal with breakpoints at $-3$, $-1$, $2$, and $4$, identify the reflected breakpoint locations and the new interval order for $x(-t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Given breakpoint values at $-3$, $-1$, $2$, and $4$, the cue for time reversal is to reflect each breakpoint across $t=0$ first. Do not rewrite any segment formulas yet; this step only changes the breakpoint locations.
Now sort the reflected breakpoints from left to right on the time axis. The order is determined by the new positions after reflection, not by the original order of the values.
So the breakpoint list for $x(-t)$ is $-4$, $-2$, $1$, $3$. Stop here: this step ends with the reflected breakpoint locations and their left-to-right order only.

sections.section_title: Substituting $-t$ Into Piecewise Segment Formulas

example_content.example_prompt: A two-piece signal has $2t+1$ on $[-2,1)$ and $4-t$ on $[1,3]$. Rewrite the formulas in $x(-t)$ and keep the reflected interval order from the previous step.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the reflected interval order from the previous step. Keep that order fixed and substitute $-t$ into each segment formula; this step changes the algebra inside the pieces, not the breakpoint locations.
Start with the left-hand formula $2t+1$ and the right-hand formula $4-t$. Replace every $t$ with $-t$ in each one and simplify the signs.
Attach the simplified formulas to the reflected intervals from left to right. The piece with $4+t$ belongs on the left, and the piece with $-2t+1$ belongs on the right.
So the new work in this step is formula substitution and simplification. The interval order stays fixed from the previous step; the formulas change by replacing $t$ with $-t$.

sections.section_title: Reordering Reversed Piecewise Intervals

example_content.example_prompt: A three-piece signal uses $1$ on $[-4,-1)$, $t+2$ on $[-1,2)$, and $3-t$ on $[2,5]$. Rewrite $x(-t)$ in increasing time order.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the reflected interval set from the previous steps. After time reversal, the pieces do not stay in the original order, so sort the new intervals from smallest to largest $t$ before writing the final piecewise definition.

Reflect the intervals first. The original rightmost piece on $[2,5]$ becomes the leftmost piece on $[-5,-2]$, the middle piece on $[-1,2)$ becomes $(-2,1]$, and the original left piece on $[-4,-1)$ becomes $(1,4]$.
Now write the pieces left to right in the new order: $[-5,-2]$, $(-2,1]$, $(1,4]$. The formulas stay attached to their reflected intervals.

The new skill in this step is ordering the reflected intervals before you write the piecewise definition. The formulas do not move on their own; they follow the interval that each reflected piece belongs to.

sections.section_title: Reversing a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal

example_content.example_prompt: A four-piece signal is $0$ on $[-5,-2)$, $t+1$ on $[-2,0)$, $2-t$ on $[0,3)$, and $4$ on $[3,6]$. Find the complete piecewise definition of $x(-t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the complete reversal procedure from the previous steps. First reflect the breakpoints, then substitute $-t$ into each formula, and finally sort the transformed pieces from left to right.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(t)=\begin{cases} 0, & -5\le t<-2 \\ t+1, & -2\le t<0 \\ 2-t, & 0\le t<3 \\ 4, & 3\le t\le 6 \end{cases}

explanation_blocks.text: Reflect the breakpoints one piece at a time. The transformed intervals appear in reverse order: $[3,6]\to[-6,-3]$, $[0,3)\to(-3,0]$, $[-2,0)\to(0,2]$, and $[-5,-2)\to(2,5]$.
Now substitute $-t$ into each formula and simplify. The constant pieces stay constant, while the affine pieces change by sign inside the variable term.
Write the pieces in increasing time order: $[-6,-3]$, $(-3,0]$, $(0,2]$, $(2,5]$. Attach the simplified formulas to those intervals in that same left-to-right sequence.

This example combines all three operations: reflect the breakpoints, substitute $-t$ into every segment, and then sort the transformed intervals. The answer is correct only when the formulas and intervals are matched together in the final left-to-right order.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert an exponential signal $x(t)=Ae^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ into $x(-t)=Ae^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ and interpret the result as reversing growth or decay and complex-rotation direction.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Reversal of Exponential Signals

blocks.text: Time reversal means replacing every $t$ in the signal with $-t$. For exponential signals, that substitution flips the sign in the exponent, so the same rule controls both growth or decay and complex rotation.
Start with the real-exponential base case, where $\omega=0$. Replacing $t$ by $-t$ gives $x(-t)=Ae^{-\sigma t}$, so a positive $\sigma$ becomes decay and a negative $\sigma$ becomes growth.
The same substitution works for a pure complex exponential. When $x(t)=Ae^{j\omega t}$, time reversal flips the sign of $\omega$, so the rotation direction in the complex plane reverses.
After reversal, $x(-t)=Ae^{-j\omega t}$. The magnitude stays the same, but the direction of rotation is opposite.
For the full exponential $x(t)=Ae^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$, time reversal combines both effects at once. The result is $x(-t)=Ae^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$, which later examples can reuse one part at a time.

sections.section_title: Time Reversal of a Pure Real Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=4e^{3t}$. Find $x(-t)$ and decide whether the resulting signal grows or decays as $t$ increases.

explanation_blocks.text: Since this is the base case with $\omega=0$, use the substitution rule from the previous step: replace every $t$ with $-t$ and then simplify. The amplitude stays the same; only the exponent changes.
Apply the rule directly: $x(-t)=4e^{3(-t)}$. This is the same signal with time reversed, so the positive exponent now points in the opposite direction.
Now simplify the exponent to get $x(-t)=4e^{-3t}$. The coefficient $4$ does not change, because time reversal acts on $t$, not on the amplitude.
Because the exponent is negative, the signal decays as $t$ increases. The reversal has turned the original growth into decay, which is exactly what the substitution rule predicts.

sections.section_title: Growth and Decay After Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=5e^{-2t}$. Find $x(-t)$ and explain how the growth or decay behavior changes after reversal.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a decaying real exponential, so use the same reversal rule as before: replace $t$ with $-t$ and keep the coefficient unchanged.
Substituting $-t$ gives $x(-t)=5e^{-2(-t)}$. The only change is the sign on the time variable inside the exponent.
Simplify the exponent to get $x(-t)=5e^{2t}$. The amplitude stays $5$, but the sign flip reverses the exponential behavior.
The original signal decays as $t$ increases, while the reversed signal grows as $t$ increases. The sign of the exponent is what controls the classification after time reversal.

sections.section_title: Time Reversal of a Pure Complex Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=2e^{j4t}$. Find $x(-t)$ and identify the new rotation direction in the complex plane.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same substitution rule as before: replace every $t$ with $-t$ and simplify the exponent. Here the cue is a pure complex exponential, so the only thing that changes is the sign of the imaginary frequency term.
Substitute $-t$: $x(-t)=2e^{j4(-t)}$. The amplitude stays $2$.
Simplify the exponent to get $x(-t)=2e^{-j4t}$. The sign of $\omega$ has flipped, but its magnitude is unchanged.

Because the sign of the imaginary exponent reversed, the phasor rotates in the opposite direction in the complex plane. Time reversal changes only the direction of rotation, not the size of $\omega$ or the coefficient.

sections.section_title: Rotation Direction After Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=3e^{-j5t}$. Find $x(-t)$ and state whether the phasor now rotates clockwise or counterclockwise.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same substitution rule: replace every $t$ with $-t$ and then simplify. The cue here is a pure complex exponential, so the sign of $\omega$ determines whether the phasor is clockwise or counterclockwise.
Substitute $-t$: $x(-t)=3e^{-j5(-t)}$. The coefficient stays $3$ and the magnitude of $\omega$ stays $5$.
Simplify to get $x(-t)=3e^{j5t}$. The original negative sign on $\omega$ has flipped to positive, so the direction of rotation flips with it.
Because $e^{-j5t}$ rotates clockwise as $t$ increases, the reversed signal $e^{j5t}$ rotates counterclockwise. Time reversal swaps the direction while preserving the frequency magnitude.

sections.section_title: Time Reversal of a General Complex Exponential

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=4e^{(2+j3)t}$. Find $x(-t)$ and explain how time reversal changes both the amplitude trend and the rotation direction.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the time-reversal rule: replace every $t$ with $-t$. That flips the entire exponent, not just the real part or just the imaginary part.
The factor $e^{-2t}$ means the amplitude now decays as $t$ increases, and the factor $e^{-j3t}$ means the phasor rotates in the opposite direction from the original signal.
So the reversed signal keeps the same scale factor $4$, but both behaviors flip together: a growing, counterclockwise exponential becomes a decaying, clockwise one.

entries.lesson_core_move: Map each original signal time point $t_0$ to $t=(t_0-b)/a$ for $x(at+b)$ to interpret the combined shift, scale, and possible reversal of a continuous-time signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Combined Shift and Scale Operations

blocks.text: Start with one labeled time point in $x(t)$ and a positive scale factor. For $y(t)=x(at+b)$, read the transformed signal by asking which original time point $t_0$ satisfies $t_0=at+b$.
Solve that relation for $t$ to locate the same feature in the transformed signal: $t=(t_0-b)/a$. This inverse map is the rule you will reuse for every labeled time point.

Keep the roles separate: $a$ controls compression, expansion, and possible reversal, while $b$ controls the shift after scaling is accounted for. If $a<0$, the same inverse map flips the order of the time points.

Apply the same inverse map to every endpoint or labeled feature, and you get the transformed support interval or any other multi-point description without changing notation. The symbolic rule stays the same point by point.

sections.section_title: Mapping Key Time Points for $x(at+b)$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ has labeled landmarks at $t_0=0$, $t_0=4$, and $t_0=8$, and let $y(t)=x(2t-4)$. Find the transformed times of those landmarks in $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the inside argument of $x$ in $y(t)=x(2t-4)$. Read each landmark by setting the original time $t_0$ equal to that argument, so $t_0=2t-4$.
Solve that relation for $t$ to get the inverse map $t=(t_0+4)/2$. This tells you where any labeled time point in $x(t)$ appears in $y(t)$.
Now substitute the labeled times from $x(t)$: $t_0=0$ gives $t=2$, $t_0=4$ gives $t=4$, and $t_0=8$ gives $t=6$.

explanation_blocks.latex: t_0=0 \Rightarrow t=2,\quad t_0=4 \Rightarrow t=4,\quad t_0=8 \Rightarrow t=6

explanation_blocks.text: Because $a=2>0$, the order stays the same in the transformed signal. The landmarks appear at $t=2$, $t=4$, and $t=6$ in that order.

sections.section_title: Finding the Transformed Support Interval

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,6]$ and let $y(t)=x(3t-6)$. Find the support of $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the support interval of $x(t)$, which runs from $t_0=0$ to $t_0=6$. Use the same inverse map from the previous step and apply it to both endpoints of the interval.
Map the left endpoint first: when $t_0=0$, the transformed time is $t=2$. Then map the right endpoint: when $t_0=6$, the transformed time is $t=4$.

Because $a=3>0$, the order of the endpoints stays the same, so the transformed signal is nonzero on $[2,4]$. The support is obtained by transforming both endpoints and writing the result in increasing order.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Combined Compression and Shift

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,8]$ and has landmarks at $t_0=0$, $t_0=4$, and $t_0=8$. For $y(t)=x(4t-8)$, find the transformed support and describe how the spacing between the landmarks changes.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the interval support together with the landmark spacing in $x(t)$. Read $y(t)=x(4t-8)$ by setting the original time equal to the inside argument, so $t_0=4t-8$.
Solve for $t$ to get the inverse map $t=(t_0+8)/4$. This map tells you where each original landmark lands in the transformed signal.
Now map the endpoints and the middle landmark: $t_0=0$ goes to $t=2$, $t_0=4$ goes to $t=3$, and $t_0=8$ goes to $t=4$.

explanation_blocks.latex: t_0=0 \Rightarrow t=2,\quad t_0=4 \Rightarrow t=3,\quad t_0=8 \Rightarrow t=4

explanation_blocks.text: Because $a=4>0$, the order stays the same, but every spacing is divided by $4$. The support becomes $[2,4]$, and the transformed signal is compressed in time while the whole interval shifts right.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Combined Expansion and Shift

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,4]$ and let $y(t)=x(0.5t-1)$. Find the support of $y(t)$ and describe the change in width.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the support interval of $x(t)$, which runs from $t_0=0$ to $t_0=4$. Use the same inverse map as before and apply it to both endpoints of the interval.
Map the left endpoint first: when $t_0=0$, the transformed time is $t=2$. Then map the right endpoint: when $t_0=4$, the transformed time is $t=10$.

Because $a=0.5<1$, the order of the endpoints stays the same, but the width doubles from $4$ to $8$. The transformed signal is nonzero on $[2,10]$, and the whole interval shifts right while expanding in time.

sections.section_title: Handling Negative Scale Factors in $x(at+b)$

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ has labeled landmarks at $t_0=2$, $t_0=4$, and $t_0=6$, and let $y(t)=x(-2t+6)$. Find where those landmarks appear in $y(t)$ and state the order they appear in.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative scale factor in $y(t)=x(-2t+6)$ and the labeled times $t_0=2$, $t_0=4$, and $t_0=6$. Use the inverse map $t=(t_0-b)/a$ with $a=-2$ and $b=6$, so the transformed time is $t=(6-t_0)/2$.

Now apply that rule to each landmark. The point at $t_0=2$ moves to $t=2$, the point at $t_0=4$ moves to $t=1$, and the point at $t_0=6$ moves to $t=0$. The mapped times descend as the original times increase, which is the reversal check.

explanation_blocks.latex: t_0=2 \Rightarrow t=2,\quad t_0=4 \Rightarrow t=1,\quad t_0=6 \Rightarrow t=0

explanation_blocks.text: If $t_0=2$ and $t_0=6$ are the support endpoints, then the transformed support is written in increasing order as $[0,2]$. The interior landmark still lands at $t=1$, but the left-right order is flipped by the negative scale factor.

entries.lesson_title: Order of Operations in Signal Transformations
entries.lesson_core_move: Sequence time shifts, time scaling, and time reversal correctly when converting between a continuous-time signal's transformed expression and its resulting graph.

sections.lesson_title: Order of Operations in Signal Transformations
sections.section_title: Introduction to Order of Operations in Signal Transformations

blocks.text: The object to watch is the transformed argument inside $x(\cdot)$. When the signal is written in factored form, as $y(t)=x(a(t-b))$, read the factor $a$ first and the shift $b$ second.

To locate where an original feature at time $t_0$ appears in the transformed signal, solve the inside relation $a(t-b)=t_0$. That gives the inverse map $t=t_0/a+b$, which is the rule you will reuse for every labeled time point.

Use the base case $y(t)=x(2(t-1))$ to see the order clearly. The factor $2$ compresses time by $2$, and the $-1$ inside the parentheses shifts the compressed signal right by $1$, so a feature at $t_0$ lands at $t=t_0/2+1$.

If $a<0$, the same inverse map still works, but the order of the landmarks reverses because the signal has been flipped in time before the shift is read. Before you compare a formula to a graph, factor the argument first, then read the factor, then read the shift.

sections.lesson_title: Order of Operations in Signal Transformations
sections.section_title: Sequencing a Shift and Positive Time Scale

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=8$ and let $y(t)=x(2(t-1))$. Find where the peak appears in $y(t)$ and state the order of operations that produced it.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factored inside argument of $x$ in $y(t)=x(2(t-1))$. Read the factor $2$ first: it compresses time by a factor of $2$ before the shift is applied.
Set the original time equal to the inside argument, then solve for $t$. This gives the inverse map $t=t_0/2+1$, which tells you where any labeled time point appears in the transformed signal.
Now apply the rule to the peak at $t_0=8$. Substituting gives $t=5$, and the peak height stays the same because only the time location changes.
So the peak appears at $t=5$. The order is scale first, then shift: compress by $2$, then move right by $1$. The factor $2$ acts before the $-1$ inside the parentheses is read as the shift.

sections.section_title: Sequencing a Shift and Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=6$ and let $y(t)=x(-2(t-1))$. Find where the peak appears and explain how the reversal changes the order of landmarks.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factored inside argument of $x$ in $y(t)=x(-2(t-1))$. Read the minus sign first: it flips time, not amplitude, so the factor acts as a reversal before the shift is applied.
Set the original time equal to the inside argument, then solve for $t$. This gives the inverse map $t=1-t_0/2$, which is the rule you reuse for every labeled time point.

Now apply the rule to the peak at $t_0=6$. Substituting gives $t=-2$, and the peak lands on the opposite side of $t=0$ because the negative scale factor reverses the time order before the shift is read. The peak height stays the same.
So the peak appears at $t=-2$. The order is reversal first, then shift right by $1$: flip by the negative scale factor, then apply the shift inside the parentheses.

sections.section_title: Factoring an Unfactored Time Argument Before Transforming

example_content.example_prompt: Suppose $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[0,8]$ and let $y(t)=x(4t-12)$. Factor the argument and find the support of $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unfactored argument inside $x$ in $y(t)=x(4t-12)$. Rewrite it first so the scale-and-shift order is visible before you map the support.
Now set the original time $t_0$ equal to the inside argument and solve for $t$. This gives the inverse map $t=(t_0+12)/4$, which is the rule you reuse for every endpoint of the support.
Apply the map to the original support endpoints $t_0=0$ and $t_0=8$. They go to $t=3$ and $t=5$, so the transformed signal is nonzero on the interval between those times.
So the support of $y(t)$ is $[3,5]$. Factoring first reveals the order: scale by $4$, then shift right by $3$.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a plotted source signal $x(t)$ with a peak at $t=6$ and support $[0,8]$, and a transformed graph with the peak at $t=5$ and support $[2,6]$, recover the operation order that produced the graph.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pair of graphs. Compare the support width and the landmark positions to recover the operation order from the picture.

On $x(t)$, the support runs from $0$ to $8$, so the width is $8$. On $y(t)$, the support runs from $2$ to $6$, so the width is $4$. That means the time axis was compressed by a factor of $2$ before the shift.
With that scale factor, the inverse map is $t=t_0/2+2$. It sends the peak at $t_0=6$ to $t=5$.
So the graph comes from scale by $2$ first, then shift right by $2$. The transformed peak at $5$ and support $[2,6]$ match that order.

example_content.example_prompt: Compare the graphs produced by $y_1(t)=x(2(t-2))$ and $y_2(t)=x(2t-2)$ for the same source signal, and explain how the different order changes the peak location and support.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both graphs come from the same source signal, so the only thing that changes is the order of the same shift and scale operations. Compare the peak and support placements to see which order produced each graph.

For $y_1(t)=x(2(t-2))$, read the factor $2$ first. Scaling by $2$ compresses the original support width from $8$ to $4$ and moves the peak from $t_0=6$ to $t=3$; shifting right by $2$ then gives support $[2,6]$ and peak $5$.
For $y_2(t)=x(2t-2)$, start with the shift. Shifting right by $2$ moves the support to $[2,10]$ and the peak to $8$; scaling by $2$ then compresses that graph to support $[1,5]$ and peak $4$.
So the two orders are not interchangeable: scale-then-shift gives peak $5$ and support $[2,6]$, while shift-then-scale gives peak $4$ and support $[1,5]$.
